definition: Platitude means a stale, unoriginal remark.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word platitude. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know platitude should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The fortune cookie offered its usual platitude — 'every journey begins with a single step' — which felt thin beside a dinner this good.
A remark is neutral ground — maybe fresh, maybe dull; it stops well short of platitude on the staleness scale.
A commonplace goes further than a plain remark toward wear — everyone has heard it before — but a platitude completes the slide: worn smooth, posing as wisdom, saying nothing.

A bromide is a soothing, stale saying handed out like a pill — meant to calm the moment rather than to enlighten it. A platitude poses as wisdom; a bromide only means to comfort. Both are worn out, but the platitude pretends to depth while the bromide pats your hand.

A proverb is a worn saying that still earns its keep — 'measure twice, cut once' is old and still saves lumber. A platitude is a saying that has stopped working: worn smooth, posing as wisdom, delivering none. Age ripens a proverb; it only wears a platitude smoother.
a fresh observation that actually opens something up
a polished, witty saying that still surprises

Platitude means a stale, unoriginal remark.
The graduation speaker had twelve minutes and used them on platitudes: follow your passion, reach for the stars, be true to yourself.
The valedictorian, given three, told one true story about the school's janitor — and hers was the speech parents quoted at dinner.
A platitude is a remark worn featureless by use: once wise, now automatic, offered where thinking should go.
It differs from a proverb, which stays useful, and from small talk, which never claimed depth — the platitude poses as wisdom while delivering none.
Platitude is an accusation: the remark is stale and pretending to be wise.
Bromide is gentler, commonplace gentler still; a cliche can be any overused phrase, not just mock-wisdom.
Praise no one's platitudes — if the saying still earns its keep, call it a proverb or an adage instead.

Our yearbook adviser banned one sentence outright: 'Never change.' It was, she said, the emptiest platitude in the building -- a line that sounds warm, costs nothing, and means nothing, since everyone signing it will be different by August.
She posted a challenge instead.
A signature earned its ink only if it named one specific thing: the bus-stop joke, the lab fire, the exact seat in the exact row.
Stripped of stock phrases, seniors sat chewing their pens like first graders.
By June the books read like tiny biographies, and not one page told anybody to stay exactly the same forever.
